articles.title: Sandblasting grit: why 320 shows die-cast porosity
articles.excerpt: Sandblasting fixes the feel of an aluminium surface with one number: the grit. 120 grit reads matte with visible tooth. 220 grit is fine and even. 320 grit comes close to silk, with very low reflectio…
articles.body: Sandblasting fixes the feel of an aluminium surface with one number: the grit. 120 grit reads matte with visible tooth. 220 grit is fine and even. 320 grit comes close to silk, with very low reflection. Across that range 60-degree gloss lands between 2 and 10 GU and surface roughness between Ra 1.6 and 3.2 micrometres. Grit sets the baseline. Finer is not better. Sand cast and die cast aluminium carry porosity and flow marks, and coarse to medium grit from 120 to 220 covers them; at 320 those defects come back into view. So choosing a grit is really choosing between hiding defects and getting a fine touch, and the two rarely come together. Appearance parts usually want the even matte of 320, and pay for it with fingerprints, which means a clear coat or an anodised seal on top.

articles.title: Go Sequencing Windows — Containing Partial Batch Failures on a Delivery Tracking Map
articles.excerpt: A live map has one constraint that changes the design: after a disconnect, the client must distinguish an event it never received from an event it received and then lost from memory. A faster transpor…
articles.body: A live map has one constraint that changes the design: after a disconnect, the client must distinguish an event it never received from an event it received and then lost from memory. A faster transport cannot answer that question. Only an ordered, replayable delivery contract can. Short answer: Assign every device-status event a stable identity and a monotonic position within its stream, acknowledge batch members individually, and reconnect from the last contiguous position rather than the largest position observed. That choice treats a batch as a transport envelope, not a transaction. If positions 410 through 419 arrive and 414 fails validation, the dashboard may render later positions provisionally, but its durable checkpoint remains 413.

articles.title: Sector Heat Rolling Window Comparison: Unit-Testing AI Theme Heat from 1h to 3d
articles.excerpt: An AI-related concept ranks second on the one-hour heat board and eleventh on the three-day board. Is that a sudden burst, or a theme cooling off? Usually it is neither. It is two rolling windows meas…
articles.body: An AI-related concept ranks second on the one-hour heat board and eleventh on the three-day board. Is that a sudden burst, or a theme cooling off? Usually it is neither. It is two rolling windows measuring different things, and the gap only becomes a story when someone compares them without checking that the comparison is valid. This article treats a sector heat rolling window comparison like code under test. Instead of a reading checklist, we write assertions: a capture function that pulls all windows for one theme, a set of checks that must pass before anyone describes the result, and a small vocabulary for describing the shape once it does. The examples use Lava's concept heat board, and every number is illustrative.

articles.title: Three-Layer Strategy Validation and the Blind Spot That Bit Me
articles.excerpt: Three-Layer Strategy Validation and the Blind Spot That Bit Me My validation stack had three layers, and all three were green. DSR came out at 1.000. Coin-block Monte Carlo showed a 0% ruin rate acros…
articles.body: Three-Layer Strategy Validation and the Blind Spot That Bit Me My validation stack had three layers, and all three were green. DSR came out at 1.000. Coin-block Monte Carlo showed a 0% ruin rate across hundreds of randomized pool combinations. Split-half stability was positive in both halves of the trade sequence. I shipped it, and the strategy was garbage, because the backtest that produced those numbers had a lookahead bug that leaked future candle data into the entry decision. The uncomfortable lesson: all three layers evaluate the statistical properties of one trade sequence . They assume that sequence was generated honestly. None of them audits how trades were generated.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.
